newsitem.title: USA: Cocktail shakers make trendy collectibles.
newsitem.headline: Cocktail shakers make trendy collectibles.

text.p: If that New Year's Day hangover is still fresh in mind, probably the last thing you want to hear about is barware.
But as it happens cocktail shakers are back, people are collecting and prices are rising.

The fascination? Experts say it seems to be a few things: a new generation seeking the elegance of the Jazz Age, people's interest in the "finer things," and a general fed-upness with 1980s correctness.
"We're sick of white wine and fish and frozen yogurt," said Stephen Visakay, a leading collector of vintage shakers. "If you're going to have a good drink before dinner, make it a good martini."
"There's been a whole resurgence of interest in the martini and cocktails," said Gary Regan, a wine and spirits writer who lives in Cornwall-on-Hudson, about an hour north of New York City.

"And if people are going to drink martinis, they want to make them in wonderful shakers and drink them from tall, thin-lipped cocktail glasses. It's a bit of a rebellion against political correctness."
Glassware makers and retailers have responded to the trend, and new cocktail sets can be found at many department and speciality stores. Only recently that was not the case.
At the same time, demand for the new has sparked interest in the old.

"Shakers are are coming back now for the home bar," said Ray Foley, publisher of Bartender magazine. "It ties in with everybody smoking cigars and trying to look cool. The cocktail will stay and that's why shakers are back."
Foley said shakers in unusual shapes will prove most desirable: dumbbells, penguins and fire extinguishers, bowling pins, bullets and golf bags.
Prices have jumped in recent years and many Art Deco models with sleek, streamlined styling can cost a few hundred dollars. The rarest models can fetch many times that.

Visakay said he recently paid $4,000 for a rare sliver-plated airplane cocktail shaker made in Germany in the 1930s. The 18-piece set -- it contains cups, spoons, funnel, strainer and so on, with the airplane body the actual cocktail shaker -- is probably worth closer to $7,000, he said.
But more modestly priced models can be found. And luck and hard work can bring big rewards.

Visakay said his wife found a sleek "Empire" cocktail shaker at a thrift store for $5 not long ago. The chrome shaker, made by Revere in the late 1930s, can easily fetch $300 to $400 from most dealers and collectors, he said.

"If you want to start collecting, just follow your eye," said Visakay, 57, who married fellow collector Arlene Lederman in June after they'd met at a flea market -- both reaching for the same cocktail shaker -- some 10 years earlier.
Visakay counts 1,400 shakers in his collection and regularly lends items to museums. He says Arlene was the best thing he ever found at a flea market.
You can find shakers at antique shows and dealers, but "it'll cost you," Visakay said, recommending flea markets, garage sales and the like as better hunting grounds.
A cobalt glass dumbbell with silver trim was advertised as "the most natural way to shake a cocktail" by Wanamaker's department store in New York in 1936. It can fetch $300 to $400.
A red glass shaker shaped as a woman's leg, also made by the defunct West Virginia Speciality Glass Co., is worth $450 or more, Visakay said.
He recommended looking for aluminum models and industrial designs as well as brightly coloured shakers from the 1950s, which he called especially good buys.
For example, a glass 1950s shaker with a pink and black rooster on it can be found for $40 or $50. Visakay thinks it will double in price.
A show with 95 pieces from his collection is to open on Sunday at the Louisiana State Museum in New Orleans.
His book, "Vintage Barware" (Collector Books, $24.95), is due out in June. Call (800) 626 5420.
To subscribe to Bartender magazine, call (800) 463-7465.
Regan's "The Book of Bourbon and Other Fine American Whiskeys" (Chapters, $29.95), co-written with his wife, deals with whiskey, not cocktail shakers. It can be ordered by calling (800) 892-0220.
